value.0: You still land loud on the third step. Everything else has gone quiet. There is nothing left for you on my range - one round, one answer, wherever you carry it. Waste neither.

Fourteen steps from the door, nine of them wasted motion. Your rifle isn't done teaching you yet. When it hangs off you like part of your spine - when the shot is the last thing you do instead of the first - come back. I'll hear the difference before you knock.

Eleven steps, and the fourth was loud. Sit anyway. There's a crew squatting in the Czerka Arms Test Range - the old proving lanes here on the Smuggler's Moon - burning rounds like breath is free. Their adepts call what they do my doctrine. It isn't. Six of them on the near lanes. Put them down and bring me the One Shot Czerka Test Docket they score themselves against. I want to see what they think counts as a hit.
The key in your hand opens the range gate - Czerka stamped it, I kept it. Down the landing, near lanes first. Wind runs left to right past the third marker. You didn't ask. Now you know.

A round is a promise. You spend it, something ends - the fight, the argument, the animal's pain. Spray, and you're a liar with a rifle. One breath, one round, one answer. That's the whole doctrine. It takes a lifetime.

Range crew. Czerka let them stay on when the contracts dried up, and they found my old target logs and decided doctrine was a thing you could copy off paper. Now they teach it loud and sell it louder. Six adepts on the near lanes. They count their hits. They never count their misses. That tells you everything.

The One Shot Czerka Test Docket. Their trial record - scores, groupings, round counts. I want the round counts. You can't shame a man with words on this moon; words are cheap here. Numbers, though. Numbers are honest.
Six adepts. One docket. The near lanes. You're spending words I didn't buy - go spend rounds instead.
The near lanes went quiet. Quiet is the correct sound. Show me the paper.

Two hundred six rounds between six shooters. Eleven scored hits. I've seen weather shoot better. Payment's counted out in your account - once, like everything I do. Rest your shoulder. The next lanes are longer.

Five specialists hold the mid-lanes. Better than the six you dropped - these miss with intention. They pulled the blast-cell regulator off the line and cranked every test rifle hot, because a hot rifle flatters a bad shooter. Take all five and bring back the One Shot Blast-Cell Regulator. Rifles should tell the truth.
Mid-lanes, past the first checkpoint. They work in pairs - one spots, one sends. Break the pair and the second shot never comes. Wind dies at midday down there. Go at midday.

In volume. A specialist puts five rounds in the air hoping one lands honest, and against most people one does. Don't be most people. Between the third and fourth trigger pull there's a breath. Live inside it.

Overcharged cells flatten the arc and lie about range. Every shot feels like a gift - until the cell burns out mid-fight, or the barrel does, or the man does. The One Shot Blast-Cell Regulator kept those rifles honest for twenty years. They silenced it because honest rifles kept scoring them low.

I don't. Czerka is a ledger with a flag on it. But those lanes taught me my trade, and a rifle that lies raises liars. Someday somebody stands downrange of those students and pays for the lesson. I'd rather it was nobody.
Five specialists. One regulator. Midday, when the wind lies down. Everything else is stalling.
You walk different when the weight is real. It's riding high on your pack - I heard it against the frame at the door. Let's see it.

Twenty years it metered those lanes. It'll meter twenty more. The range log says you spent forty-one rounds this week; a month ago it would have read ninety. You're learning what spending means. Payment's counted.

The warden holds the long lane, and he wears the One Shot Scored Range Crest. My crest - the one I shot for, back before he decided wearing it was the same as earning it. He is patient. The real kind, not the counterfeit. So hear me: one trigger is not enough down there. One trigger, many eyes. Take two spotters you'd trust with your own breath, or don't go at all. The last shooter who walked that lane alone is still on it. Nobody has managed to go fetch him.
Good answer. Set your spotters wide, and shade the glass - he reads scopes off glare. He will wait for your first miss and answer it, so don't miss first. Simple to say. Costs everything to do.

I set the lane record the year that crest was struck. When I walked away, Czerka needed somebody to wear it for the clients, and he was the best still standing. He wore it so long he forgot the difference between the record and the man who set it. I don't want it back for the record. I want it back because everything it touches goes rotten on him.

Nine hundred meters. A crosswind that changes its mind three times along the way. Cover that works only until he's ranged it - which takes him one shot. That's why you bring eyes. A man can only be patient in one direction at a time.

Patience isn't armor. It's a bet that you break before he does. Three shooters who don't break, moving on separate breaths, and the bet's already lost. He'll know it, too. Around the second exchange he'll start spending rounds he meant to keep. That is the sound of a patient man dying. It sounds like hurry.
The warden is still on the long lane, and my crest is still on the wrong shoulder. Your spotters still breathing? Then all that's missing is the walk down.
One shot this morning. Just the one. The whole moon is quieter for it. Show me the crest.

Hm. Lighter than I remembered. Twenty years on the wrong man makes metal heavy - I didn't know it worked the other way too. Keep those spotters close. What's left down there doesn't fight in lanes anymore. It fights in packs.

Four of the old crew left - the inner circle, the ones who taught the rest to spray. They've sealed the deep lanes behind a pooled clearance chit and they're stripping the range as they go. Optics, charge cells, twenty years of target logs. Mine among them. Take all four and bring me the One Shot Czerka Clearance Chit. It's the last key that isn't yours.

Four rounds. I'll hold you to the arithmetic. They move together, room to room, covering corners the way the warden covered distance - so bring the same eyes you took to the long lane. Short lanes kill faster than long ones. Less time to be wrong.

Close work. Everything the long lane wasn't. They clear rooms in a wheel, each one watching the next one's blind side. Good doctrine, stolen like the rest of it. Break the wheel at one spoke and the other three are just men in a room. Pick your spoke before you breathe the door open.

The One Shot Czerka Clearance Chit opens every gate, cage, and rack on the range. While they hold it, the range bleeds - gear out, strangers in. When you put it in my hand, the range closes. A range should have one gate and one keeper. I'm done pretending otherwise.

Eleven years of my rounds - wind, light, charge, pulse. A man's whole breath written down in numbers. In their hands it's a manual for counterfeiting me, sold by the page. Bring me the chit and they lose the armory it's locked behind. The logs I'll burn myself.
Four shooters, one chit, deep lanes. You've counted higher than four. Go count these.
Nine rounds fired down there. I counted through the floor. Four targets. I'll want an accounting of the spare five - after I see the chit.

Doors count. Barely. The range is closed now - one gate, one keeper, the way it was cut to be. Which leaves the far lane, and the man on it. I've been not talking about him since you first came in loud. Sit down. This one I'll spend words on.

Last target. The master on the far lane never joined that crew - they squatted on his range for years and he never wasted a single round telling them to leave. He is the doctrine finished. One round, one answer, every time. I watched him shoot the worst wind this moon ever threw, and I never saw him fire twice. There is nothing to carry out - his silence will be the proof. So bring every eye you trust. One trigger, many eyes, and against him the eyes matter more than the trigger, because whoever he sees first is spent.

Good arithmetic. The far lane opens past the deep lanes - the chit's gate, then walk. He won't hide; he'll be standing in the open, because for him the open is cover. Spread your breaths. Nobody moves while he's exhaling. And if it ends the way I think it can, come tell me quietly.

Once. Nine hundred meters, one round each. Mine grazed his collar. His took the sling off my shoulder without breaking skin. We agreed, without one word, that the argument was settled and neither of us had won it. I left the moon. He stayed. That's the whole story, and you're the first person I've spent it on.

Because he stopped answering to anything. That crew hung his silence on every hit contract on this moon, and he let them - silence signs anything if you never spend words. A round is a promise, and he's forgotten who he was promising. What's left is just the shot, going wherever it's paid to go. The doctrine has to pass to somebody who still keeps the promise part. You, if you live.

You don't beat the shot. You spend it. Three of you means his first round buys him one target instead of the fight, and no man alive is reloading and untouchable in the same breath. That breath is the entire battle. Your eyes call it, your trigger closes it. He would tell you the same. He may yet - he talks to the ones who make it interesting.
The far lane is still occupied. I'd know otherwise - this moon sounds different when he's gone. Gather your eyes. Spend them well.
There it is. Thirty years I've listened to this moon, and this morning it finally exhaled. One shooter left standing on the far lane, and it's you. Say it plain.

Then the range is yours - the doctrine, the quiet, all of it. He kept the promise to the very end; now it's yours to keep. I've counted every round you've spent since you first walked in loud. The number is good. Make every one after it count for something.
Back to the job.
Six adepts. Every round will count.
What is your doctrine, then?
Who are they?
What's in the docket?
Not today.
The One Shot Czerka Test Docket. Their numbers are ugly.
Back to the lanes.
Five. And the regulator comes home.
How do they shoot?
What does a hot rifle change?
Why do you care what Czerka's rifles do?
My barrel needs rest first.
The One Shot Blast-Cell Regulator. The rifles tell the truth again.
Back to the long lane.
One trigger, many eyes. I'll bring mine.
How did he end up with your crest?
What makes the long lane different?
How does a patient man lose?
I don't have my eyes yet.
The One Shot Scored Range Crest. Off the warden's shoulder.
Back to the four.
Four targets. Four rounds, if I'm honest about it.
What do these four do differently?
Why does the chit matter to you?
What's in the logs they're stripping?
Not until I've read the wind on this one.
The One Shot Czerka Clearance Chit. Two of the spares went into a door lock.
Back to the far lane.
Then he sees three of us. And none of us first.
You watched him shoot. Did you ever face him?
If he's the doctrine finished, why does he need to die?
How do we take a man who doesn't miss?
Not until every one of my eyes is ready.
It's done. He got his one answer.
